title: A cost on competency restores a Baldwin effect and genetic assimilation

fields.label: Label
fields.value: A cost on competency restores a Baldwin effect and genetic assimilation

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: In the 1D artificial embryogeny model, penalizing fitness in proportion to competency (penalty factors 1×10⁻⁷ to 0.5) produced a Baldwin effect: structural-gene fitness kept improving, selection favoured progressively lower competency, and early competency-based gains were assimilated into the structural genes; the authors note real competency costs are unmeasured.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: Cellular Competency during Development Alters Evolutionary Dynamics in an Artificial Embryogeny Model

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Shreesha L 2023, Cellular Competency during Development Alters Evolutionary Dynamics in an Artificial Embryogeny Model › 3. Results › 3.5. A Fitness Penalty for Competency Leads to Continued Improvement of an Embryo’s Structural Genes

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Thus early gains based on the competency gene are later assimilated into the structural genes, paralleling what has been described previously in the context of organism-level learning [59].

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Shreesha L, Levin M, “Cellular Competency during Development Alters Evolutionary Dynamics in an Artificial Embryogeny Model”, Entropy (Basel, Switzerland) (2023), doi:10.3390/e25010131; section “3. Results › 3.5. A Fitness Penalty for Competency Leads to Continued Improvement of an Embryo’s Structural Genes”. Scope: In silico 1D artificial embryos with a fitness penalty on competency

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on levin-2023-competency-09: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.87

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The claimed Baldwin effect is an explicit pattern among model variables and is reproducible from published methods. This resolves the in-silico statement, not whether real developmental competency has such costs.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Run the model across the stated competency penalties and track structural-gene fitness, competency, and phenotypic fitness over time. Genetic assimilation is supported when structural fitness rises as competency declines while phenotype remains high.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The conclusion depends strongly on the chosen cost function.

Actual biological competency costs are not represented by existing data.

operationalizability: 0.98

discriminating power: 0.94

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The penalty rule and the factor range are stated, and the underlying simulator is public, so the Baldwin runs can be reimplemented as an extension rather than a new kind of model. They are not a packaged experiment in the repository, and some controls sit in the supplement. The in silico claim is testable with that extra assembly; it does not measure real competency costs.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Subtract a penalty proportional to competency, over factors from 1e-7 to 0.5, from fitness in the public evolvable-competency loop, and track structural-gene fitness and the competency allele. Continued structural improvement, declining competency and later genetic assimilation would confirm the simulated Baldwin effect; competency staying high, or structural fitness stalling, would refute it at that cost.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The public scripts and hyperparameter file do not expose the fitness-penalty experiment as a turnkey run.

Real organismal costs are unmeasured, so the simulation does not say which penalty factor is biological.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

analysis feasibility: 0.55
operationalizability: 0.84
data adequacy: 0.58
data existence: 0.62
